questions.text: I notice the precise moment when a group conversation becomes dominated by one person.
I tend to choose the restaurant, the movie, or the activity that I most want.
I can handle multiple stressors simultaneously without feeling destabilized.
I do not usually notice when someone is carefully not mentioning a person or topic that is obviously relevant.
I compare estimated time versus actual time on tasks to improve my planning accuracy.
I sense when a team member is withdrawing their investment in a project through subtle disengagement.
After a stressful event, it takes me a long time to return to my emotional baseline.
I keep a running list of things I need to remember and review it regularly.
I proactively organize shared spaces and group projects because order enables progress.
I notice when a person arranges their belongings on a table to claim space or establish boundaries.
When I hear about a group of people in serious trouble, I usually feel some concern for them.
I tend to weigh how a decision affects me before considering how it affects others.
Even after hearing the whole story of what a person has endured, I feel little wish to help them.
Even when I clearly understand another person's hardship, their wellbeing rarely becomes more important to me.
I feel most like myself when I am in the middle of helping someone.
I rarely feel emotionally overwhelmed, even during genuinely difficult times.
A messy desk doesn't bother me; I know where everything is in my own way.
I tend to miss when someone uses a particular anecdote to send a message to someone else in the group.
I rarely consider whether the timing of a message carries meaning beyond its content.
I routinely offer to drive others to appointments, even when it disrupts my own plans.
I am the person who reframes a problem so the team can act on it.
I send emails as soon as I write them, trusting my first phrasing is good enough.
I let the day's most important task reveal itself through my engagement rather than deciding it in advance.
When I'm emotionally activated, my peripheral vision narrows and everything feels urgent.
Suffering among people outside my own circle rarely concerns me.
I rarely overrule a group decision, even when I think there is a better option.
I find that traveling alone to pursue my own interests is more fulfilling than compromising on a group itinerary.
When I have a vision, I pursue it whether or not others initially agree.
As I work through the details of another person's difficulty, I care about what the experience is like for them.
I ask the group to define what done looks like before we begin.
I often wait for the group to signal readiness before pursuing change.
When I learn that someone has been harmed, I feel a moral pull to respond that remains present until I have taken action.
When I feel content, the contentment saturates me completely — it's not a background hum, it's the whole song.
I tend to be the voice that names the elephant in the room.
I tend to respond to every request for help before attending to my own inbox.
My nervous system seems to have a wide comfort zone that few experiences push me out of.
